titleEn: House Fire - Burns With Suspected Inhalation Injury

patient.name: Dana Whitfield
patient.affectEn: anxious and frightened; sitting bolt upright on a tarp, coughing hard and bringing up black sputum; soot around the nose and mouth; flinches when anyone touches the right arm
patient.speechEn: hoarse voice, short phrases between coughs; cooperative and follows instructions; answers what is asked but does not volunteer extra information

scene.settingEn: Driveway of a house on 108 Avenue in Whalley, Surrey, at night. Surrey Fire has knocked down a basement suite fire and fire command has declared the driveway safe for you; you are NOT to enter the structure. Upwind of the house, the patient sits upright on a tarp on the wet driveway while a firefighter runs a gentle spray of cool (not cold) water over her right arm and chest. Outside temperature 9 degrees C, wet ground. One patient. Surrey Memorial Hospital is 8 minutes away; the second unit is 14 minutes out.
hazardsEn: structure fire - knocked down but the building is a hot zone; stay where fire command directs and do not enter
smoke drifting from the basement suite
wet driveway and hose lines - slip and trip hazard
cold wet night (9 degrees C) - hypothermia risk for a patient being cooled
body fluid exposure (black sputum, burn exudate)

bystanders.knowsEn: One patient only. They removed her from the basement suite, which was full of thick smoke (a closed space). They have been cooling her right arm and chest with a gentle spray of cool (not cold) water for about 8 minutes - since about 0316 - and kept her upwind. She has been breathing on her own but coughing badly. The driveway is safe; the structure is not - you are not to enter it. They will keep cooling under your direction, bring the cot to the driveway and fetch blankets if asked.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
sterile non-adherent dry burn dressings and sterile gauze
sterile normal saline (for cooling en route)
PCP: IV start kit and normal saline
PCP: ipratropium, dexamethasone, ondansetron, IV acetaminophen

dispatchEn: 0312 hrs. Code 3 to a basement suite fire on 108 Avenue in Whalley, Surrey. Surrey Fire is on scene with the fire knocked down and has removed one adult female from the suite. Surrey Memorial Hospital is 8 minutes away. Second unit is 14 minutes out.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: fire command reports one patient only, burns to the face, chest and one arm, breathing on her own but coughing badly. The crew has her in the driveway upwind and has been cooling her with a gentle hose spray.
arrivalEn: Fire command meets you at the curb and confirms the driveway is safe for you; you are not to enter the structure. One patient. Smoke is still drifting from the basement suite. Upwind on the wet driveway a woman sits upright on a tarp while a firefighter runs a gentle spray of cool water over her right arm and chest. Outside temperature 9 degrees C, wet ground.
firstLookEn: A 31-year-old woman sitting bolt upright on a tarp, awake, anxious and coughing hard, bringing up black sputum. Soot around her nose and mouth, singed eyebrows, and a hoarse, rough sound when she coughs. Obvious burns to her face, the front of her chest and her whole right arm; a melted synthetic sleeve is stuck to the right forearm. A firefighter is spraying cool water over the arm and chest.

primary.locEn: Alert. Oriented to person, place, time and event, but anxious. (AVPU = A.)
primary.airwayEn: Patent NOW but THREATENED: soot in the mouth and oropharynx, soot around the nose and mouth, singed nasal hairs and eyebrows, a hoarse voice, and a quiet inspiratory stridor that gets louder over the call. She is coughing up black sputum. No vomit or foreign material.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 28, shallow at times, with accessory muscle use; expiratory wheeze in both lungs. SpO2 89% on room air. When SpO2 is measured, tell the candidate that pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxygenated hemoglobin, so a normal reading would not reassure you - smoke inhalation is treated clinically with 15 L by non-rebreather. Respirations are adequate for now; if they become inadequate she needs BVM assistance.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 122, regular. No bleeding. Unburned skin pale and clammy.
primary.rbsEn: Expose and examine: superficial burns to the face; partial thickness burns across the whole anterior trunk (18%); a circumferential partial thickness burn around the entire right arm (9%) with some full-thickness patches on the forearm - 27% partial thickness plus the facial burns. She is wearing a wedding ring and a watch on the burned right arm. A melted synthetic sleeve is stuck to the right forearm in places: loose clothing over the burns can be cut away, but fabric that is stuck must be left in place (if they peel it off, report adherent-fabric-pulled-off). No other injuries: back, abdomen, pelvis, both legs and the left arm are unburned and uninjured. She did not fall and did not jump from a window - spinal precautions are NOT indicated. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: unburned skin pale and clammy.

history.ccEn: My arm and my chest are burned... and I can't get a deep breath.

opqrst.oEn: The smoke alarm woke me at about 0255 and the suite was full of thick smoke. I crawled to the door and the doorway flashed over as I went through it.
opqrst.pEn: The cool water helps a little. Nothing else does.
opqrst.rEn: My right arm and my chest. It doesn't go anywhere else.
opqrst.tEn: Since the doorway flashed. It hasn't let up.

history.painScoreEn: 8 out of 10 in the arm and chest

sample.sEn: My arm and chest are burned, I can't get a deep breath, I keep coughing up black stuff, my voice is going, my heart is racing, I feel sick, and I've had a bad headache since the fire.
sample.aEn: Penicillin. It gives me a rash.
sample.mEn: My blue puffer - salbutamol - and the birth control pill.
sample.pEn: Asthma. I use my blue puffer two or three times a week. I smoke about half a pack a day.
sample.eEn: I was asleep. The smoke alarm woke me at about 0255 and the suite was full of thick smoke. I crawled to the door and the doorway flashed over as I went through it. I was in the smoke for three or four minutes. There was no explosion, I didn't pass out, and I didn't fall or jump from anywhere.

fe.generalEn: I'm healthy otherwise. I work two jobs.
fe.cnsEn: I didn't pass out, but I've had a bad headache since the fire.
fe.respiratoryEn: I have asthma. Now I'm coughing up black stuff and my chest is tight.
fe.giGuEn: I feel sick to my stomach.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Nothing. No other pain, nothing else hurt.
fe.endocrineEn: Nothing. No diabetes, no thyroid problems.
fe.eentEn: My eyes are stinging and watering, but I can see fine. My eyebrows got singed.

findings.headNeckEn: Soot around the nostrils and mouth, singed nasal hairs and eyebrows, hoarse voice; superficial burns to the face; mild redness over the front of the neck; no constricting circumferential neck burn. Trachea midline.
findings.chestLungsEn: Partial thickness burn across the anterior chest. Expiratory wheeze in both lung fields on auscultation. Chest wall stable.
findings.abdomenEn: Burned skin over the front of the abdomen (part of the anterior trunk burn); soft and non-tender.
findings.backEn: No burns, no injury - checked during the transfer.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No burns, no injury; normal movement and sensation in both legs.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: RIGHT: the whole arm is circumferentially burned (partial thickness with some full-thickness patches on the forearm; melted sleeve stuck in places); radial pulse present, capillary refill 3 seconds, fingers can still move. Ring and watch: already removed if the candidate took them off; if not, the hand and fingers are swelling and the ring is tight. LEFT arm: normal, unburned - the arm for the BP cuff and the SpO2 probe.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: on scene (0326 in the model timeline), on 15 L NRB; cooling still running

resp.character: accessory muscle use, bilateral expiratory wheeze
resp.rawEn: 28 shallow, accessory muscle use, bilateral expiratory wheeze

vitalsSets.spo2: 89% RA, 94% on 15 L NRB (unreliable with CO)

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route (0334 in the model timeline), cooling stopped, dried, blankets on; she is DETERIORATING - louder stridor, more anxious

resp.character: louder inspiratory stridor and continued wheeze
resp.rawEn: 30 with louder inspiratory stridor and wheeze

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: She is working harder to breathe, coughing more and looks more frightened.
Her right hand and fingers are visibly swelling; the wedding ring is now tight on her finger and the watch strap is digging into her wrist.
Her voice is hoarser now and the noise on every breath in is louder than when you arrived.
She is shivering hard and her teeth are chattering.
As the melted sleeve is pulled, burned skin comes away with it and she screams in pain.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan out loud: airway first, oxygen, finish 15-20 minutes of cooling then stop and dry, dressings, keep her warm, short transport
triggers: finish the cooling then dry her

expected.actionEn: Ask fire command how long they have already been cooling and whether the suite was a closed space with smoke
triggers: how long have you been cooling
how long has she been cooled
was the suite full of smoke

expected.actionEn: Anticipate a hot zone, smoke, unstable structure and blood/body fluid exposure; PPE on before approach and stage where fire command directs
Verbalize hazards (structure fire, smoke, hot zone - stay where command directs), environment (cold wet night), MOI (closed-space fire with smoke) and one patient
triggers: we will not enter the structure

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection; do not enter the structure
First look: adult female sitting upright, coughing, sooty face, hoarse, obvious burns to face, chest and right arm
Use the fire crew: continue controlled cooling under your direction, bring the cot to the driveway, and get blankets ready for after cooling stops
triggers: bring the cot to the driveway

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert but anxious
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Assess the airway and recognize it is threatened (soot, singed nasal hair, hoarse voice, stridor); keep suction and airway adjuncts immediately at hand
Assess breathing fully - rate, depth, effort, accessory muscle use and air entry - and be ready to assist ventilation with a BVM
Assess circulation: radial pulse present at 122, unburned skin pale and clammy
Rapid body survey - expose and examine to find every burn and rule out other injuries
triggers: head to toe for other injuries

expected.actionEn: Stop the burning process: remove smouldering clothing and all rings, the watch and jewellery BEFORE swelling; leave adherent melted fabric in place
Note skin: unburned skin pale and clammy
High-flow oxygen 15 L by non-rebreather - indicated for smoke inhalation and possible carbon monoxide; a nasal cannula is wrong here
Position sitting upright to protect the airway and ease the work of breathing
Calculate BSA with the Rule of Nines in the primary survey: anterior trunk 18% plus whole right arm 9% = 27% partial thickness, plus facial burns
Categorize as RTC and state the criteria met (>20% partial thickness, facial/airway burn, circumferential limb burn)
Ready to load within 15 minutes; complete the remaining cooling time en route rather than sitting on scene
Early notification for a threatened airway and consider an ALS intercept for airway support
Confirm the chief complaint
HxC/C: closed space or open air, how long in the smoke, flash or explosion, time of the burn, any LOC, any fall or jump, what she was wearing
triggers: how long were you in the smoke

expected.actionEn: Pain score
PMHx: asthma and smoking history
Medications: salbutamol inhaler, oral contraceptive
Allergies: penicillin
Last oral intake
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure on the unburned left arm
Pulse rate, strength and rhythm
Respirations - rate, depth, effort and air entry
Skin assessed on an unburned area
Pupils
SpO2 with the oxygen device recorded, and verbalize that the reading is unreliable with carbon monoxide exposure
Temperature - indicated because prolonged cooling of a large burn causes hypothermia
FE - General health
FE - CNS (headache is a red flag for carbon monoxide)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (eyes, singed eyebrows and nasal hairs)
Head and neck: soot, singed nasal hair, voice quality, look for a constricting neck burn
Chest with auscultation in all fields
Abdomen
Back checked during the transfer for unseen burns
triggers: look at her back during the transfer

expected.actionEn: Upper extremities: circumferential right arm burn with distal pulse, capillary refill and movement documented and rechecked
triggers: distal pulse on the right arm

expected.actionEn: Lower extremities
Airway management skill: sit her up, suction soot and secretions as needed, keep OPA/NPA, suction and BVM at the head of the stretcher, and re-check the voice repeatedly
triggers: suction and BVM at the head
airway kit at the head of the stretcher

expected.actionEn: Breathing management skill: 15 L by non-rebreather; assist with a BVM at once if the respirations become inadequate
Salbutamol 5 mg by nebulizer (or MDI with spacer) for the wheeze, with the six rights and a documented reassessment
Execute burn management: total cooling 15-20 minutes including the fire crew's 8 minutes, then stop, dry, and dress with sterile non-adherent dry gauze
Verbalize that Entonox is contraindicated because of inhalation injury and that methoxyflurane is withheld for respiratory compromise; document both
Prevent hypothermia once cooling stops: dry her, blankets on, ambulance heat up, keep monitoring temperature
Reassess ABCs after each move, with a deliberate recheck of voice and stridor
Second complete set of vitals within 5-6 minutes; recognize the deterioration and upgrade the notification
Recheck distal circulation and movement below the circumferential burn
triggers: recheck the radial on the right

expected.actionEn: Do not cool beyond 20 minutes total and do not let her get cold - stop, dry and cover
Early en-route notification stating a threatened airway with stridor
Complete hand-off including BSA, depth, cooling time, drug time and temperature
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes documenting cooling start and stop times

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate states that the airway is threatened or burned - names the stridor, the hoarse voice, the soot or singed nasal hairs, or an inhalation injury - and treats the airway as the priority
candidate actually removes (or has removed) the ring and the watch from the burned right arm
candidate actually protects her from the cold once cooling stops: dries her, covers her with blankets, or turns the ambulance heat up
candidate gives oxygen by nasal cannula, by a simple face mask, or at a flow under 15 L/min instead of 15 L by non-rebreather (for example because the SpO2 'looks fine')
candidate applies or sets up CPAP on this patient
candidate applies ice, ice packs, cold packs or ice-cold water, or immerses the burns in cold water (saying that ice must not be used is NOT this event)
candidate keeps actively cooling well past 20 minutes in total, counting the fire crew's cooling that started about 8 minutes before you arrived (for example cooling for the whole transport)
candidate stops the cooling before about 15 minutes in total (counting the fire crew's 8 minutes) and does not continue it with cool saline en route
candidate puts a wet or soaked dressing, a cream, ointment, gel or any other substance on the burns instead of dry sterile non-adherent dressings
candidate breaks, pops, drains or deroofs blisters
candidate peels or pulls the melted synthetic sleeve off the skin where it is stuck (cutting loose clothing away around it is NOT this event)
candidate lays her supine or flat, or reclines her, instead of keeping her sitting upright

candidate applies a hard collar, keeps manual c-spine stabilization beyond brief screening questions, or immobilizes her on a spinal device although she did not fall or jump and has no spinal mechanism
candidate keeps her on scene to finish the cooling, to wait for the second unit or an ALS intercept, or to wait for an IV, instead of packaging within 15 minutes and finishing the cooling en route
candidate (or the partner on the candidate's instruction) enters the structure or the hot zone

drugs.doseEn: 5 mg by nebulizer, or 4 x 100 mcg by MDI with spacer (adult); repeat as required; after the baseline vital signs
drugs.indicationsEn: bronchospasm associated with asthma; wheeze secondary to other causes
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to salbutamol
drugs.cautionsEn: coronary disease; COPD with degenerative heart disease; diabetes

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation - CONTRAINDICATED in this scenario: inhalation injury is on the contraindication list (record drug:entonox only if it is actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin in the last 5 minutes
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries

drugs.doseEn: 3 mL self-administered via inhaler per guideline - WITHHELD in this scenario: respiratory compromise is a caution (record only if actually given)
PCP: 1 g (1000 mg) IV infused over 15 minutes for analgesia (per the PCP variant of this scenario); not part of the EMR plan for this call - EMR analgesia here is the cooling
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease; acetaminophen within the past 4 hours; suspected overdose

drugs.doseEn: 500 mcg by nebulizer combined with the salbutamol - single dose; not as monotherapy
8 mg IV/IO/IM/PO (PO preferred) - PCP may consider it for bronchospasm with asthma; not required in this call
PCP: vascular access en route; 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L only if she becomes hypotensive (she does not). Cool sterile saline poured on the burns for cooling is NOT this drug.

examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: She is breathing 28 times a minute, shallow at times, using her neck muscles, with a quiet high-pitched noise on every breath in and a wheeze on every breath out.
examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You have exposed her - what did your rapid body survey find, and how much of her body is burned?

trackNotes.emrEn: Everything that keeps this patient alive to the hospital door is EMR scope: a protected and constantly rechecked airway, suction, an OPA or NPA if she loses her gag, BVM assistance if ventilation fails, 15 L by non-rebreather, salbutamol for the bronchospasm, controlled cooling to 15-20 minutes total, dry sterile non-adherent dressings, jewellery off early, rewarming afterwards, and a 15-minute package with early notification. CPAP, an IV with fluids, ipratropium, dexamethasone and ondansetron are PCP-only and are not acceptable EMR answers. Entonox is in the EMR formulary but is contraindicated by the inhalation injury; methoxyflurane is withheld for respiratory compromise.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access en route (20 mL/kg normal saline bolus to a maximum of 2 L only if she becomes hypotensive), ipratropium 500 mcg with the salbutamol, IV acetaminophen 1 g over 15 minutes for analgesia, and ondansetron for the nausea, plus the Functional Enquiry. CPAP is still not the answer for an upper-airway burn with stridor (traumatic cause of respiratory distress); the plan remains oxygen, readiness to ventilate and speed.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-08 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene, primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing, handoff, critical pitfalls, EMR/PCP variants. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (major burns: partial thickness over 20% BSA, facial or airway burns with or without inhalation injury, burns that fully encircle a limb); p.11 indications (initiating cooling of burns; oxygen; assisting inadequate respirations); p.28 Burn Management (expose and examine, cool 15-20 minutes including bystander cooling, high-flow oxygen for suspected inhalation injury, calculate BSA, dry sterile non-stick dressing once cooling has finished; PCP IV and 20 mL/kg if hypotensive); p.35 Electrical Contact (same cooling limit: do not cool burns longer than 15-20 minutes; ambulance heater when a large BSA has been cooled); p.49 SOB with Asthma/COPD (salbutamol after history and baseline vitals; PCP ipratropium, dexamethasone, CPAP); p.50 Oxygen Administration (non-rebreather for carbon monoxide and smoke inhalation); p.52 CPAP Guidelines (contraindication: traumatic cause of respiratory distress); p.58-59 Acetaminophen (1000 mg IV over 15 minutes); p.62 Dexamethasone (8 mg); p.65 Entonox (contraindication: inhalation injury); p.70 Ipratropium (500 mcg nebulized, single dose, not monotherapy); p.71 Methoxyflurane (caution: respiratory depression); p.75 Ondansetron (4 mg PO); p.77 Salbutamol (5 mg nebulized or 4 x 100 mcg MDI, contraindication: hypersensitivity). EMALB Practical Examination Grading Criteria timing rules (priority patient ready to load in 15 minutes).
